summary: Because RFC 3966 says tel URIs cannot represent a dial string, there was no standard way to give one in a SIP address. This memo adds a new value, dialstring, for the user parameter of sip and sips URIs so that user=dialstring can carry it. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Some phone numbers are really button presses to dial, not names. This adds a label so computers can tell which is which.

questions: what is a sip dial string
what is user=dialstring in a sip uri
what does phone-context do in a sip uri
what do p and x mean in a dial string
subtitle: A new user=dialstring value that lets a SIP URI say its user part is keypad input, not a phone number.

tldr.problem: RFC 3966 says tel URIs cannot represent a dial string, and a SIP URI user part made of dial-string characters cannot be told apart from one that just happens to use the same characters.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a new value, dialstring, for the user parameter of sip and sips URIs. A URI with user=dialstring must also carry a phone-context parameter naming the dialing plan.
tldr.outcome: Intermediaries that own the context can translate the dial string into a telephone number or a service URI. Dial strings should normally stay inside the domain of the user agent client.

facts.label: P and X
facts.value: P is a pause, X waits for call completion

today: RFC 4967 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Dial String Problem
sections.content:
A user at a phone often has a limited interface, sometimes only a 10 key pad and a flash function. The digits the user enters are called a dial string. It may be translated to a telephone number, or it may invoke a special service.

Many newer designs hold the mapping from dial string to number or service URI inside the phone (a digitmap). Phones and terminal adapters without such a mechanism must send the dial string in a sip: or sips: URI to an intermediary that knows the dialing plan and can transform it.

The catch is that the intermediary can only do this if it recognizes the user part as a dial string. Today nothing distinguishes a dial string from a user part that merely uses the same characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine handing someone a note with just numbers on it. They cannot tell if it is a phone number or the buttons you pressed on a machine. This memo adds a label to the note.

sections.title: DTMF Tones and Voicemail Strings
sections.content:
The RFC also points to DTMF (dual tone multi-frequency) detectors that are used after the first number has been dialed. Some systems express a string that includes fixed time delays, or an actual wait for call completion, after which more DTMF signals are sent.

Many voicemail systems work this way: they use a common phone number and then expect the desired mailbox number as a series of DTMF digits. Many gateways can interpret such strings, but there is no standardized way to write them down, which leads to interoperability problems between endpoints. Being able to say that a dial string is being presented helps here too.
sections.plainLanguage: Some phone systems want you to dial a number, wait, and then press more buttons. This gives everyone one agreed way to write that down.

sections.title: Requirements for Expressing a Dial String
sections.content:
The RFC requires a way to express a dial string in a sip: or sips: URI. A dial string is a sequence of the digits 0-9, the special characters pound and star, the DTMF digits A-D, and characters for a short pause and for a wait for call completion.

The A-D digits come from the fourth column of the DTMF 4 x 4 matrix, which is not used in the PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network). Some systems do use them, so they are included.

Two more requirements apply. A dial string always exists within a context, and the context MUST be specified. It also MUST be possible to tell a dial string from a user part made of the same characters.
sections.plainLanguage: A dial string can hold number buttons, star, pound, and a few extra tones, plus a pause. It must always say which phone system it belongs to.

sections.title: The user=dialstring Parameter
sections.content:
The solution is a new alternative value, dialstring, for the user parameter of the sip: and sips: URI schemes. The dial string uses the characters 0-9, A-F, P, X, star and pound. Here E stands for star, F stands for pound, P is a pause (a short wait, like a comma in a modem string) and X means wait for call completion.

When user=dialstring is used, a phone-context parameter as defined in RFC 3966 MUST be given. It would normally be a domain name. That name does not have to resolve to a host, but it MUST be under the administrative control of the entity managing the local phone context. The value is normally configured in the user agent. It sits between the digits and the @ in the userinfo.

A dial string SHOULD NOT be used for an address of record in a REGISTER. Parameters are ignored in registration, so two registrations with different phone contexts would look equivalent, which is probably not desirable.
sections.plainLanguage: The label is called user=dialstring. Letters stand in for the special buttons, and a note says whose phone system the numbers belong to.

sections.title: Translation and Examples
sections.content:
A proxy server or Back to Back User Agent that is authoritative for the context may translate the dial string into a telephone number or a service invocation URI. The number MAY be written as a global or local tel: URI, or it MAY stay a sip: or sips: URI with the parameter changed to user=phone.

The RFC gives two examples. The first is what a SIP phone might emit when a user dials extension 123. The second is a voicemail case, where a local access extension is followed by the mailbox number sent as DTMF using X.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper at the phone company reads the button presses and turns them into a real phone number or a service.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Dial strings exposed to the Internet may reveal internal network details or service invocations. That could let attackers use the PSTN or the Internet to attack internal systems. Dial strings normally SHOULD NOT be sent beyond the domain of the UAC (User Agent Client). If they are sent across the Internet, they SHOULD be protected against eavesdropping with TLS (Transport Layer Security) as described in RFC 3261.

On the IANA side, RFC 3969 defines a SIP URI parameter sub-registry in which the user parameter has predefined values. This RFC adds the value dialstring and is added to the references for that parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: Button presses can give away secrets about a company's phone system, so they should stay inside the building or travel in a locked box.
